claims.text: HEA protective-coating wear performance is governed by formation of a stable nanocrystalline surface oxide layer.
The protective nanocrystalline oxide layer can develop during service.
The protective nanocrystalline oxide layer can be pre-engineered.
A stable nanocrystalline oxide layer reduces friction during abrasive contact.
A stable nanocrystalline oxide layer reduces material removal during abrasive contact.
Controlled heating in an oxygen-containing atmosphere can form a uniform nanocrystalline oxide layer on an HEA coating.
Oxide-film thickness, continuity, and crystallinity are the structural variables mediating wear performance.
The pre-formed oxide layer acts as a barrier that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Reduced direct metal-to-metal contact lowers friction and wear.
The oxide layer improves resistance to material removal by abrasive wear.
The oxide layer improves resistance to material removal by adhesive wear.
Under identical wear conditions, pre-oxidized coatings will have lower friction coefficients than as-deposited coatings.
Under identical wear conditions, pre-oxidized coatings will have lower wear rates than as-deposited coatings.
The proposed protective effect should hold from room temperature to approximately 100°C when the oxide remains stable.
The protective effect is limited to loads and temperatures that do not cause oxide spallation or breakdown.
Oxide spallation or breakdown eliminates the oxide's protective effect.
The optimum oxide thickness, grain size, and phase composition may depend on HEA composition and service conditions.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes regimes in which the oxide spalls or breaks down, but the falsification rule treats irreversible oxide degradation or spallation as falsifying the hypothesis without requiring that it occur inside the stated load-and-temperature stability regime. Spallation outside that regime would confirm the boundary rather than falsify the bounded hypothesis.
